CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep negotiating the draft text without new unilateral concessions or a fresh retaliatory package. Trade purchase volume and limited legal/IP language for a written path to freeze List 3 at 10% and begin removing existing Section 301 duties; reject a U.S.-only snapback that leaves the $250B tariff wall in place. Do not reopen the tariff war this week, and keep the Huawei/Meng track legally and diplomatically separate from the trade text so a commercial deal is not held hostage to an unresolved criminal case.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high-crisis. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is still ~$250B (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%), and China already matched on ~$34B, ~$16B, and then 5–10% on ~$60B of U.S. goods; that is a material hit to export sectors, not a symmetric nuisance. Firm-level tech pressure is also live: Meng Wanzhou remains in the Canadian extradition process after the 1 Dec 2018 arrest and the 28 Jan 2019 DOJ fraud/sanctions indictment of Huawei and Meng, which China treats as an attack on a national champion. Those two facts pull the reading toward the +0.5 CHN anchor. What keeps it well below that anchor is the real-economy picture as of late April: Q1 2019 GDP held at 6.4% (top of the 6–6.5% target), March industrial production jumped 8.5% y/y, surveyed urban unemployment eased to 5.2%, CNY strengthened to about 6.72 from ~6.96 in late October, and reserves are stable near $3.11T. Seasonally adjusted Chinese merchandise exports are only modestly softer over the window; the sharper signal is bilateral—U.S. goods imports from China fell from $46.3B (Nov) to $34.5B (Apr), about −26%—so export hubs are feeling the tariffs even while stimulus has stabilized the headline. Action should therefore be negotiate, not escalate or concede. The 1 Dec G20 truce and Trump’s 24 Feb delay already suspended the scheduled List 3 hike to 25%; April 3–5 Washington talks reported line-by-line progress on text, including enforcement language, with Trump saying a deal/summit call would be known within about four weeks. Remaining blockers, per contemporaneous U.S. and Chamber reporting, are exactly the ones that would make a premature Chinese concession costly: Washington wants tariffs as an enforcement/snapback tool and has floated leaving the $250B duties on after a deal, while Beijing is pushing for their removal. Unilateral purchase commitments or structural lock-in without a matching tariff path would trade away industrial-policy space for no relief; a new Chinese tariff or non-tariff blast now would give Washington an easy pretext to restore the 25% List 3 hike just as markets are calm (VIX ~13) and both presidents are signaling they want a deal. Hold is too passive given active drafting; partial_rollback or concede_purchases is premature until the U.S. puts comparable tariff relief on the table.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports remain under Section 301 tariffs; List 3 25% hike is only suspended, not cancelled
Huawei/Meng criminal-extradition track is unresolved and sits outside the trade text
Q1 2019 GDP 6.4%, March IP +8.5%, firmer CNY and stable reserves reduce immediate economic desperation
Bilateral U.S. imports from China are already down ~26% since November — export-hub pain is real even if headline growth held
April talks are in endgame drafting; remaining fight is enforcement/snapback vs removal of existing U.S. tariffs
Escalating now risks restoring the List 3 25% hike; conceding purchases/structure without tariff relief would lock in a bad bargain

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
Intensive Washington talks between US and Chinese negotiators; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
CNY/USD latest 6.7207 on 2019-04-24, down from 6.9605 on 2018-10-29 (−3.4%) — yuan stronger, not under FX-crisis pressure.
China reserves ex-gold ~$3,114bn in April 2019, up ~1.1% over the window — no reserve drain.
US goods imports from China fell from $46.3bn (Nov 2018) to $34.5bn (Apr 2019), about −25.6%.
China industrial production index 108.5 in March 2019 then 105.4 in April — still expanding y/y, not a collapse.

Trump: we'll know over the next four weeks if a deal happens. Sides still disagree on using tariffs as an enforcement tool; Trump has said tariffs on $250bn could stay even after a deal; China has pushed for removal.
US Chamber: week of April 3 talks critical; unlikely China would agree to an enforcement mechanism that re-imposes unilateral US tariffs without current tariffs being removed.

Q1 2019 GDP +6.4% (above 6.3% consensus, top of 6.0–6.5% target); March IP +8.5% y/y, strongest since July 2014; urban jobless 5.2% in March. Stimulus offsetting trade-war hit; unsigned deal remains largest uncertainty.
Canadian government allowed Meng extradition process to go forward (1 Mar 2019); diplomatic standoff continues, Canadians detained in China.
